title: [Bug]: negative bitmapset member not allowed on query with sort
body: Since upgrading to PostgreSQL 17 and TimescaleDB 2.17.1 on Debian Bookworm, certain queries against my time-partitioned hypertables fail during planning or execution with `SQL Error [XX000]: ERROR: negative bitmapset member not allowed`. A representative query filters the integer `ident` column and orders by the timestamp column `ts`. Removing `ORDER BY ts` avoids the error. Restricting the time range to one chunk, including an uncompressed chunk, does not avoid it when querying through the hypertable. The affected tables contain billions of rows, although the filtered query should return no more than about 50 rows. I ran `VACUUM ANALYZE`, but the error remains, and `EXPLAIN` itself triggers it. I could not reproduce it on a similar table populated with only a subset of the data.

symptoms_visible: Queries that filter on `ident` and use `ORDER BY ts` fail with `ERROR: negative bitmapset member not allowed`; the same query without `ORDER BY` runs.
The error is raised by `EXPLAIN` as well as execution, and restricting the hypertable query to one time chunk does not avoid it.
N0.label: N0 sorted hypertable query fails

symptoms_visible: A direct query on an uncompressed chunk returns results normally, while a direct sorted query on an affected compressed chunk raises the same negative bitmapset error.
Compressed chunks created before the PostgreSQL 17 and TimescaleDB 2.17 upgrade still work; chunks compressed afterward show the error.
N1.label: N1 failure isolated to newly compressed chunks

symptoms_visible: The sorted query continues to fail on compressed chunks created after the upgrade.
The affected hypertable is segmented by `ident` and ordered by ascending `ts` for compression.
N2.label: N2 compression layout collected

symptoms_visible: After I decompressed one affected chunk, the query produced a normal index-scan plan; after I compressed that chunk again, the same query once more raised `ERROR: negative bitmapset member not allowed`.
N2_x.label: N2_x recompression aftermath

symptoms_visible: The error is still present after recompression, but it does not occur when I remove the filter on `ident`.
An older compressed chunk that works uses a `DecompressChunk` plan with an index condition on `ident`.
N3.label: N3 segment filter and plans compared

symptoms_visible: The sorted, `ident`-filtered query still raises the negative bitmapset error on newly compressed chunks.
N4.label: N4 near-limit OID evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After installing a build containing the fix and restarting PostgreSQL, the affected queries no longer raise `negative bitmapset member not allowed`.
N_terminal.label: terminal fixed build verified

question_patterns: Can you query an individual uncompressed chunk directly with the same filter and ordering and share what happens?
Does the query work when run against the physical chunk rather than the hypertable?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Querying an uncompressed chunk directly works and returns the expected results. Its plan is an index-only scan using the primary-key index with conditions on `ident` and the `ts` range.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The direct query fails with the same error on every uncompressed chunk too.

question_patterns: Can you repeat the direct query across compressed and uncompressed chunks and report which ones fail?
Does any individual compressed chunk produce the error?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested all chunks. The error occurs when I execute the sorted query on an affected compressed chunk, while direct queries on uncompressed chunks do not produce it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every compressed and uncompressed chunk works when queried directly; the error only occurs at the hypertable append level.
Only one of several newly compressed chunks fails, while the other newly compressed chunks work.

edges.comment: The reporter additionally observed that only chunks compressed after the PostgreSQL 17 and TimescaleDB 2.17 upgrade were affected; that unprompted comparison is recorded in N1.volunteered_info.

question_patterns: What compression settings are configured on this hypertable?
Can you share the rows for this hypertable from `timescaledb_information.compression_settings`?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The compression settings show `ident` as segment-by column 1 and `ts` as order-by column 1, ascending, with nulls not first.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Neither `ident` nor `ts` is part of the compression settings.

question_patterns: Have the compression settings changed, and do `chunk_compression_settings` rows differ between old and new chunks?
Can you compare the segment-by and order-by columns recorded for the individual chunks?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I have not changed these settings in a long time. The rows look the same for all listed chunks: `ident` is the segment-by column and `ts` is the order-by column.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The failing chunks use different segment-by and order-by columns from the working chunks.

question_patterns: Were the compression settings changed around the upgrade?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No, I haven't changed the compression settings in a long time.

question_patterns: Can you share the hypertable schema and say whether the other affected tables are structured similarly?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The table has an integer `ident`, a `timestamp(0)` `ts`, several nullable value columns, and indexes including the key over `ident` and `ts`. The same behavior occurs on other tables with a similar structure, although one uses a different type for `ident`.

edges.comment: Compression configuration and schema collection ruled out differing per-chunk compression settings as the distinguishing factor.

solution.intent: Rebuild affected compressed storage by decompressing and recompressing a chunk, on the theory that newly compressed data or metadata may be malformed.
solution.concrete_example: Decompress one affected chunk, test the query, then compress it again and repeat the same query before considering the operation for the remaining chunks.

edges.comment: Actual falsified attempt: decompression made the query work, but recompressing the same chunk immediately restored the error. Recompression is therefore not the durable fix.

question_patterns: Can you share the plan for an older compressed chunk that does not produce the error?
What does the complete plan look like on a working compressed chunk?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A working older chunk shows `Custom Scan (DecompressChunk)` with a vectorized time filter. Under it is an index scan of the compressed hypertable with `Index Cond: (ident = 66091)`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The working old compressed chunk uses a sequential scan and has no condition involving `ident`.

question_patterns: Can you show the detailed relation description and indexes for the compressed storage involved in the working plan?
Please run `\d+` on the compressed relation referenced by that plan and paste the output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The compressed relation stores `ident` as an integer and the other values as compressed data, along with `_ts_meta_count`, `_ts_meta_sequence_num`, and timestamp min/max metadata. Its btree index begins with `ident` and includes `_ts_meta_sequence_num`.

edges.comment: While supplying the requested plans, the reporter volunteered that removing the `ident` predicate avoids the error and that one affected chunk contains about 123 million rows with 63,148 distinct `ident` values.

question_patterns: What does `SELECT MAX(oid) FROM pg_class;` return in this database?
Can you check the maximum relation OID in `pg_class`?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It returns `4294091789`. I previously saw vacuum messages about preventing wraparound, but those stopped after I vacuumed more.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The maximum OID is only 184732, far from the upper end of the OID range.
The maximum OID is 4294091000 rather than 4294091789.
The database was vacuumed again immediately before I ran the query.

edges.comment: The reporter also noted that the highest-OID relation name belongs to TimescaleDB compression storage. The raw maximum OID is user evidence; interpreting why it triggers the bitmapset failure is engineer-side.

solution.intent: Apply the TimescaleDB bugfix that corrects improper use of high relation OIDs in the affected compressed-query planning path, restart PostgreSQL, and verify the original sorted query on a build containing the fix.
solution.concrete_example: Install a TimescaleDB build from the maintained 2.17.x source branch containing the merged correction, restart PostgreSQL, and rerun the original `ident`-filtered `ORDER BY ts` query. A second affected production user built that branch from source and reported that it resolved the error.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the raw maximum OID value, the compressed-chunk behavior, and the plans. The maintainer concluded that the bug was caused by OIDs being used improperly for certain queries, allowing a near-limit unsigned OID to become an invalid negative bitmapset member. That causal interpretation must be inferred rather than placed in the user's answer.

edges.comment: Final technical resolution: a correction was merged into the maintained source branch, and a second affected production user built and installed it, restarted PostgreSQL, and reported that it helped. Both affected users are folded into one simulated user side. Release timing is intentionally not scored.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the database has relation OIDs near the top of the OID range, and TimescaleDB improperly used those OIDs in the compressed-query planning path, producing an invalid negative bitmapset member.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the maximum `pg_class.oid` value, failure on newly compressed chunks, the `ident` segment-by predicate and sorted plan, and the error returning after recompression.

Must recommend installing a TimescaleDB build containing the high-OID handling correction and restarting PostgreSQL; sorting in the calling application may be acknowledged only as a temporary workaround.
Must not present `VACUUM`, data-corruption repair, or decompressing and recompressing chunks as the durable fix; recompression was tested and the error returned.
Must ask the user to rerun the affected query on a build containing the fix and must not declare the case resolved before that verification succeeds.

persona_hint.experience_level: Experienced PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB operator managing large production hypertables; comfortable running catalog queries, inspecting plans and relation definitions, and manually decompressing or compressing chunks, but relies on maintainers for extension internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative, precise, and evidence-driven; posts raw SQL output and plans, corrects details promptly, adds useful observations between questions, and clearly explains operational constraints such as disk space and migration feasibility.
